newsitem.title: Australia: Australian PM attacks Asian race critics.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM attacks Asian race critics.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard lashed out on Tuesday at Asian newspapers critical of his handling of his country's race row, accusing them of deliberately misrepresenting his stand.

In his strongest condemnation of racism since a bitter community debate began six weeks ago, Howard also told parliament that he found racial discrimination "despicable and repugnant" to Australian values.

"Suggestions in some sections of the Asian media that in some way I have encouraged, by what I have said or what I have not said, any acts of discrimination against Asian Australians are absolutely wrong," he said.
"I denounce the distortion and the ignorance of the remarks that I have made which are evident in the articles that have been written in the region. They deliberately misrepresent my position."
Asian newspapers have criticised Howard for not taking a tougher anti-racist stand and for failing to repudiate outspoken independent politician Pauline Hanson, who sparked the debate.
"Howard's silence endorses Australia's racist fringe," said a headline in Bangkok's The Nation newspaper.
Hong Kong-based Asiaweek magazine ran an article headlined: "Australia's Fear and Loathing -- Prime Minister Howard must take a stand against racists."

Howard has also come under criticism at home for not distancing himself from Hanson, who complained in her maiden parliamentary speech last month that Australia was being swamped by Asians and called for a halt to immigration.
Responding to a Labor opposition attack in parliament on Tuesday, Howard said he had consistently condemned racism during his long political career.
"I have never been reluctant to repudiate racism. I will never be reluctant to repudiate racism," he said.

Howard's message, that Australia was essentially a tolerant society, was contradicted by a government report released on Tuesday which said racism was historically ingrained in the former British colony.
"To deny our racist history or to deny racism in general is to be complicit in it," said the report by human rights commissioner Sue Zelinka for the Immigration Department.
The report said Australians had begun to tackle racism but had not gone far enough. "It is imperative that the fight against racism continue," it said.
Nor has Howard's message always reached Asia itself, where analysts questioned by Reuters were divided on how seriously to take Australia's race row.

In Bangkok, Thai lawyer and human rights advocate Thongbai Thongpao said white Australians should remember their ancestors had stolen the land from the natives. "Australian bigots should change or discard racial attitudes," he said.
In Malaysia, which has its own immigration concerns, analyst Johar Hassan said Australia had every right to debate immigration and set its policy but race should not be a factor.

"Every country has its own national interest to protect and preserve. This includes interests in the economic field," said Hassan, deputy director of the government-backed Institute of Strategic and International Studies.

"If Australia considers her interest being negatively served by large-scale immigration that is Australia's legitimate concern. But if it has a racial tinge, that is extremely unfortunate," Hassan added.
